title: Iran Escalates Strait of Hormuz Attacks to Highest Level Since War Began, Threatening Global Energy Flows
snippet: Maritime attacks in and around the vital Strait of Hormuz surged in October and November as Iran seeks to disrupt U.S.-backed oil bypass routes and challenge Washington's naval blockade.
content:
Maritime violence in the Strait of Hormuz has reached its highest intensity since the war between the United States, Israel, and Iran broke out in late February, according to recent tracking data from international shipping organizations. The spike in aggression appears to be a calculated campaign by Tehran to undermine U.S.-led efforts to keep global oil supplies moving through the vital choke point.

Data from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) recorded 31 maritime attacks in and around the strait in October alone, followed by roughly 19 more through mid-November. By comparison, monthly incidents averaged between 10 and 15 from March through September. The United Nations' International Maritime Organization (IMO) confirmed a similar surge, reporting at least 34 confirmed attacks across October and November, bringing the total number of Middle Eastern vessel strikes to 138 since the conflict began.

Targeting the U.S. Bypass Strategy

The sudden escalation targets U.S.-backed workarounds designed to sidestep an Iranian-declared blockade. To keep crude moving, Washington and its regional allies have facilitated "ship-to-ship" (STS) transfers. Under this system, smaller tankers turn off their tracking transponders to navigate the strait close to the Omani coastline before transferring cargo to larger supertankers in safer waters.

"Tehran now seems determined to make these arrangements more costly and less reliable," Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said. Experts note that Iran's broader strategy is to demonstrate that normal energy exports cannot resume while the U.S. maintains its own naval blockade on Iranian shipping, which began in April.

Expanding Targets Beyond Active Crossings

Iranian strikes have not been restricted to ships actively traversing the narrow waterway. On November 8, satellite imagery confirmed a strike on the Omani island of Didamar, a strategic location hosting critical radar and satellite navigation infrastructure. Iranian state media claimed responsibility, stating it targeted "enemy navigation aid systems."

Idle ships sitting well outside the strait have also come under fire. In early October, the Panama-flagged supertanker Gem No. 2 was struck by multiple drones off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, triggering a massive fire that forced the crew to evacuate. Though Iranian state media claimed the vessel struck a naval mine while attempting an unauthorized strait passage, satellite imagery placed the ship far outside the strait. Drone warfare experts identified debris from the attack as an Iranian-made Hadid-110 jet drone.

A Broader Strategic Logic

Analysts emphasize that targeting massive crude carriers—even those anchored outside active lanes—is part of a strategic effort to discourage maritime companies from participating in U.S. safety protocols.

"Ultimately, the objective goes beyond disrupting oil exports," Azizi said. "Iran is trying to demonstrate that the United States cannot guarantee maritime security in the Persian Gulf despite its overwhelming naval superiority."

As the cycle of adaptation and counter-adaptation deepens, security experts warn that the escalating conflict poses a growing risk of broader disruptions to global energy markets and international shipping lanes.
